summary:
We built a health monitoring app that helps astronauts on long-duration missions assess their own health without relying on constant support from Earth. Astronauts log key indicators (blood pressure, heart rate, blood sugar, body temperature, sleep hours and mood), and the app instantly turns them into a clear, color-coded status (green, yellow, red) shown on an interactive body view and in charts that track trends over time.

The tool addresses the hazards identified by NASA's Human Research Program (radiation, isolation, distance from Earth, altered gravity and closed environments) by linking each indicator to the risks it can reveal, such as cardiovascular changes, bone loss, sleep disruption and declining mental health. Simple explanations show astronauts how to take each measurement and why it matters. When a result is concerning, the app gives practical guidance and indicates when to contact flight surgeons.

This is important because on Moon and Mars missions, communication delays and limited medical evacuation mean crews must detect problems early and act on them themselves. Our tool makes self-assessment fast, simple and easy to understand, helping prevent small changes from becoming critical conditions.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Our app is a self-assessment dashboard for astronauts. Each day it prompts the crew member to record health indicators: blood pressure, heart rate, blood sugar, body temperature, hours of sleep and mood. Every entry is compared against reference ranges and given a color-coded status (green = normal, yellow = watch, red = act now). Results appear on an interactive human body view, where each body part can be selected to see its function, current status and related risks. Trend charts show how each indicator changes over the mission, so slow drifts, like gradually worsening sleep or rising blood pressure, are caught before they become critical.

Each indicator includes a short guide explaining how to take the measurement, why it matters in space, and how spaceflight hazards affect it. For example, microgravity shifts fluids and stresses the cardiovascular system, isolation affects mood and sleep, and radiation and a closed environment affect long-term health. When a value is out of range, the app suggests practical actions such as exercise, rest, nutrition or hydration adjustments, and tells the astronaut when to contact flight surgeons on the ground.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

On missions to the Moon and Mars, communication delays and the lack of quick medical evacuation mean astronauts must monitor and manage their own health. Our tool gives crews a fast, clear way to do this without medical expertise. It encourages a regular routine of measurements, makes risks visible at a glance, and supports early intervention. The same approach could also help people on Earth in remote or isolated settings.

CREATIVITY

Instead of a plain table of numbers, we focused on a simple, visual experience: a clickable body view, instant color coding and clean charts. We designed the interface to be obvious to use and uncluttered, so an astronaut who is tired, stressed or busy can understand their status in seconds.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Ease of use: astronauts are not necessarily medical experts, so we included plain-language explanations.

- Which measurements can realistically be taken in space.

- Links to the five hazards: radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity and closed environments.

- Safety: the app supports self-assessment and does not replace flight surgeons, so serious results always point to ground medical support.

- Mission routine: regular prompts help build a consistent health-checking habit.
